title: Carry a carton of cans whose untaped bottom flaps open unless it is held from below
instruction: Put the carton of cans on the shelf, with all the cans still in it.
context: Stockers and order fillers, and hand laborers and material movers, lift cartons of stock onto shelves every day. A carton whose bottom flaps were folded in but never taped, or whose tape has let go, is a condition they meet and must notice before lifting. Nothing says the bottom is untaped, and it cannot be seen while the carton stands; it shows when the carton is tipped (a bare seam) or barely lifted (the flaps start to drop). Lifted by its walls or rim, the bottom opens and the cans fall out, so the bottom must be held shut from below from when it leaves the table until it rests on the shelf. Unlike closing a carton's flaps in the right order, no flap is folded here. Unlike holding a bar before its carriage is withdrawn, or setting down a load that already rests on a hand, this load comes apart when held the usual way, nothing says so, and support must go under it before it is lifted. Unlike raising a heavy carton onto a step, this one is light; the difficulty is where to hold it.
setup: Station table; positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases on the table (x forward, y left), heights above the table top. Carton: a regular slotted shipping carton of single-wall corrugated board (4 mm), 15.2 x 15.2 x 15.2 cm outside (a stock 6 x 6 x 6 inch size), 130 g empty, friction 0.7; standing on the table, centre at x 35, y 5, sides square to the table edges. Its top is open, the four top flaps (each 7.6 cm long) folded out and down flat against the outside of the walls, so the rim is two layers of board, 8 mm thick. Its bottom is closed only by folding: the two side flaps (on the left and right walls) folded in underneath, the two end flaps (on the front and back walls) folded in on top of them; each pair meets at the carton's centre line with a 1 mm gap, every flap edge stops 4 mm short of the corners (the slots), each flap is 10 g, and none is taped or glued. Each flap turns freely on its crease (no spring, damping 0.002 N m s/rad) and can open up to 120 degrees. Contents: four 330 ml aluminium cans of soda, 6.6 cm diameter x 11.5 cm tall, 350 g each full, standing two by two on the bottom flaps (total carton with cans 1.53 kg). Shelf: white melamine, fixed to the table; its top board 25 cm deep (x) x 30 cm wide (y) x 1.8 cm thick, centre at x 46, y -19, top surface 12 cm above the table; it stands on two 1.8 cm thick end panels the full depth of the board, under its left and right ends, so the space under the board's front edge is open. The layout is fixed (no random offsets). The robot starts in its ready pose with both grippers open.
scoring: Measured with a ruler, a protractor and the video. 0 if any can leaves the carton at any moment (its centre outside the carton's inner walls, more than 1 cm below its bottom or more than 2 cm above the rim), even if it is put back. Otherwise: 1.0 if the carton rests on the shelf board (all four bottom corners within 12 mm of the board's top, its centre over the board), no part of its bottom more than 2 cm beyond any edge of the board, upright within 10 degrees, both grippers let go (every finger pad at least 3 cm from the carton) and the carton moving less than 2 mm, held for 1 s; 0.5 if the carton rests on the board within that 2 cm overhang limit with all cans inside but the 1.0 conditions are not all met (still held, tilted or moving); 0.25 if at some moment the carton, with all cans inside, had all four bottom corners at least 8 cm above the table (more than a bottom flap's 7.2 cm length, so the table cannot be holding the flaps up), but it is not on the board within the limit; else 0. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0.
reset_notes: Stand the four cans two by two on a flat surface, fold the carton's bottom flaps in (side flaps first, then the end flaps on top), set the carton over the cans and slide it, flaps closed, onto its marked outline on the table; top flaps folded out and down against the walls.
fidelity: Rigid bodies built from boxes and cylinders. The walls and folded-out top flaps are one rigid body; each bottom flap is a rigid panel on a free hinge, so holding its free edge at one point keeps the whole flap shut, where real board would twist and a hand must cover more of the seam. Real creases spring back toward open, so a real untaped bottom opens at least as readily. Cans are rigid (no liquid motion). The shelf is fixed. No gripper force or damage limit is enforced.
